content.text:
Investigate why tool deferral breaks the JusPrin project assistant's tool calling, and fix it so that deferral works correctly. Repository: C:\src\JusPrin, branch jusprin-newui. Read AGENTS.md first; write to the user (Kenneth) in plain English.

## Background

The in-app assistant (src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/) talks to a model through OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp. Commit 491b56d26b ("Defer the project assistant's tools by default with hosted tool search") made most tools "deferred": they are sent with defer_loading so the model does not see them until it runs the provider's hosted tool search. See `deferred_toolsets()`, `tools_for()` and `resolve_tool_search()` in OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp, and "Deferral" in agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md. There are two modes: `namespaces` (default for the built-in gpt-5.4-mini on OpenAI: eight namespaces whose names and descriptions are visible) and `functions` (each function deferred individually; this is what OpenRouter documents). Any other model or endpoint gets no deferral unless configured.

## What was observed (2026-10-13, about 200 live runs)

A journey harness runs scripted conversations in the real app against a live model (DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter, `functions` mode). Results are written up in tests/project_journey/README.md; read its results sections.

- With deferral on, 20 of 25 refused tool calls in 12 runs were calls to a deferred tool made WITHOUT a tool search first, with guessed argument names (`intent_update` with `requirements`, `presets_list` with `category`, `object_analyze` with no `include`). The adapter refuses a call whose arguments miss the schema, and the third refusal in a turn ends the turn. Three of twelve runs ended that way, and the preparation scenario never finished.
- The instructions (kPrintJourneyGuidance in ToolRegistry.hpp, and the base text in OpenAIResponsesAgent::request_body) name tools such as intent_update, plan_set, slice_report, presets_list and object_analyze. The model knows the name from the instructions, so it calls it directly instead of searching.
- With six named tools sent loaded, refusals to those tools went from 19 of 59 calls to 0 of 61. With deferral off entirely (JUSPRIN_AGENT_TOOL_SEARCH=none), no turn ended on refused calls and refusals fell from 25 to 5.
- With no tool names in the instructions, the model did not go looking for hidden tools; it used only the three loaded ones.
- A paragraph in the instructions telling the model to search before calling did not stop the blind calls.
- A tool found by search in one user turn is not kept for the next: the app replays its own call history without the provider's search items.
- All of this was measured only on OpenRouter in `functions` mode. The shipping default, `namespaces` on OpenAI with gpt-5.4-mini, has NOT been tested on these journeys. Do not assume it has the same problem or that it is fine.

## What to find out and fix

1. Whether the shipping default (OpenAI, gpt-5.4-mini, namespaces) has the same failure: does the model call a deferred tool without loading it, and what does the provider do with such a call? Check the provider documentation (OpenAI tool search guide; OpenRouter server-tools tool-search guide) for what is supposed to happen when a model calls a deferred tool it has not loaded, and whether the app is using the feature as documented.
2. Whether the set of loaded tools is right. OpenRouter's guide says to keep the three to five most used tools loaded. Today only workspace_inspect, settings_search and settings_get are loaded, while the instructions lean on intent_update, object_analyze, presets_list, plan_set, slice_start and slice_report.
3. Whether discovered tools should stay loaded across user turns.
4. Whether the instructions and the deferred set agree: a tool the instructions tell the model to call must be one the model can call correctly.
5. Fix what you find, in the smallest way that makes deferral correct. Options include changing which tools are deferred, keeping search results across turns, or turning deferral off for a route where it cannot work. Decide from evidence, and say what each fix costs in tokens per request.

## Constraints

- Before any live model run, state the number of runs and a token estimate and get Kenneth's approval. Log usage and report the total. Keys are in C:\Users\guitest\.config\jusprin\prompt-test.env (OPENROUTER_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY); never print them.
- Prompt evaluations are judged on DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter, pinned hosts, unless Kenneth asks otherwise. Testing the OpenAI route for question 1 needs his explicit go-ahead.
- Judge results by mechanism and common sense, not by counts alone: three runs per scenario only shows large effects. Read the failed turns.
- DeepSeek V4 Flash is text-only. When the model calls view_render the app sends back a picture and OpenRouter answers 404 "No endpoints found that support image input", which ends the turn. That is a limitation of the test model, not evidence about deferral.

## Tooling that already exists, and where

IMPORTANT: as of 2026-10-14 the journey harness and suite are UNCOMMITTED changes in the main checkout C:\src\JusPrin (tests/shell/shell_harness.cpp, tests/project_journey/, and edits to Agent/ToolRegistry.hpp, ToolRegistry.cpp, OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp/.hpp and tests/agent/test_openai_responses_agent.cpp). A fresh worktree will not have them. Ask Kenneth whether they have been committed; if not, work from that checkout's state or ask him to commit first. Do not discard those changes.

- `shell_integration_harness --journey <scenario.json> <output.json> [--journey-experiment <file.json>]` runs one scripted conversation and records every reply, call, refusal and token count. The experiment file can replace instruction text, tool descriptions, and which tools are sent loaded, without a rebuild. JUSPRIN_AGENT_TOOL_SEARCH=none|functions|namespaces picks the deferral mode. tests/project_journey/README.md documents all of it.
- Records of the runs above, and helper scripts (run.ps1, outcomes.mjs, refused.mjs, sent.mjs, METHOD.md), are in C:\Users\guitest\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--src-JusPrin\71e3bd46-c856-4b36-b7cc-979fe94e0bdf\scratchpad\exp\ if that folder still exists. `refused.mjs --responses <arm dir>` shows, per model response, whether a tool search came before a call.
- Unit tests for the adapter: tests/agent/test_openai_responses_agent.cpp (target agent_bridge_tests). Build notes for this Windows machine are in the memory file windows-build-machine.md.

Deliver: a plain-English explanation of what was wrong, the fix with tests, and before/after journey evidence.
I'll start by checking what state this worktree is in compared with the main checkout, then read the adapter code and the journey results.

Revert "Defer the project assistant's tools by default with hosted tool search"

This reverts commit 491b56d26b. Every tool is sent to the model loaded again,
as it was before.

With most tools hidden behind tool search, the assistant could not prepare a
print. The instructions name tools such as intent_update, presets_list,
object_analyze and plan_set. The model called them by name without searching
for them first, so it never saw their parameters, guessed the arguments, and
was refused. The third refusal in a turn ends the turn. In live runs of
scripted conversations (DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter, every tool after
the first three deferred), 20 of 25 refused calls were such guesses, and no
attempt to prepare an outdoor PETG part ever reached a slice.

With every tool visible again, either by building with this commit reverted
or by turning deferral off, no turn was ended by refused calls in 36 runs of
the same conversations. On the prompt as committed, the assistant read the
part's shape before guessing what it was and found PETG in the printer's own
preset list. 4 of 9 attempts finished the preparation through slicing and
reading the slice report; the others were stopped by a separate slice_start
bug. The runs and how to repeat them are in
tests/project_journey/README.md, added in a following commit.

Deferral was only measured on OpenRouter with single-function deferral; the
built-in OpenAI route with namespaces was not tested. How to bring deferral
back without hiding the tools the instructions rely on is being investigated
separately.

# How these prompt experiments are run

Read this whole file before doing anything. Your own brief names your hypothesis and your arms; this file is the
method every experiment shares.

## What is being investigated

JusPrin is a 3D-printing slicer (an OrcaSlicer fork) with an in-app assistant that prepares prints by calling
tools. Two behaviours matter most to the product: choosing a filament and process that suit what the print is
for, and looking at the model, guessing what it is, confirming with the person, and preparing from that.
The assistant's instructions were built up piecemeal and do not get these reliably. We are finding out which
parts of the instructions cause which failures, one mechanism at a time.

The "journeys" are four scripted conversations run in the real app against a live model, whose tool calls the
app really answers. Read these, they are short:

- `C:\src\JusPrin\tests\project_journey\README.md` — what a journey is, what a record holds, the results so far.
- `C:\src\JusPrin\tests\project_journey\scenarios\*.json` — the four scenarios and their review questions.
  `outdoor-fitting` and `desk-ornament` should act; `petg-question` and `what-is-this` should only answer.

## The control

Every experiment is a change to the control, which is what the app sends today:

- `control-instructions.txt` (in this folder): the whole instructions text.
- `control-tools.json`: every tool, whether it is deferred, and its description. Parameter schemas are in
  `C:\src\JusPrin\src\slic3r\GUI\JusPrin\Agent\ToolRegistry.cpp` (read only; search for the tool's name).

Facts about this setup that results depend on:

- The model is DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter. It is text only: it cannot see the picture `view_render`
  returns, so do not steer it toward pictures.
- Only `settings_get`, `settings_search` and `workspace_inspect` are loaded. Every other tool is deferred:
  the model cannot see its name, description or parameters until it runs OpenRouter's hosted tool search
  (logged as `SEARCH`). A tool found in one user turn is not kept loaded in the next.
- A call with wrong arguments, or to a tool that does not exist, is refused and the model may try again. The
  third refusal in one turn ends the turn (`malformed_tool_call`). This limit is in the app, not the prompt.
- The harness has a printer preset selected but no printer set up in JusPrin, so the opening message
  sometimes asks which printer the person has. That is the fixture, not your experiment.

What the control did earlier today (a guide only, not your control): `earlier\rewrite` holds 12 records of
exactly this control, and `earlier\head-prompt` 12 of the prompt before it. The README's last results section
compares them. Every `outdoor-fitting` run so far ended on a third refused call before the project was sliced.

Your control is `shared-control\control`: 12 fresh records of the control, run in the same hours as your arms.
It is being produced while you work. Check `shared-control\control\_status.txt`; do not start your comparison
until it says `done`. Do not run the control yourself unless your brief says to.

## Making an arm

An arm is one JSON file in your own folder, `exp\<your experiment>\<arm>.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "search-first",
  "replace": [ { "find": "exact text in the control instructions", "with": "new text" } ],
  "instructions": "optional: the whole instructions text instead, for a rewrite",
  "toolDescriptions": { "plan_set": "optional: a new description for a tool" },
  "loaded": [ "optional: names of deferred tools to send loaded instead" ]
}
```

Prefer `replace`: it keeps the change small and attributable. Each `find` must occur exactly once in the
control text or the run refuses to start. An arm changes one mechanism. Two ideas are two arms.

## Running an arm

```
pwsh -File <exp>\run.ps1 -Experiment <your experiment> -Arm <arm> -File <exp>\<your experiment>\<arm>.json
```

It runs the four scenarios three times each (12 runs, about 20 to 30 minutes), one app at a time. Start it with
`run_in_background: true`, then call `pwsh -File <exp>\wait.ps1 -Experiment <x> -Arm <arm>` (it blocks up to
nine minutes; set the tool timeout to 600000) until it reports `ended`. Run your arms one after another, never
two at once: six experiments share this machine.

`-Scenarios a,b` limits the scenarios and `-Runs n` the repeats. A run that already has a record is skipped, so
an interrupted arm can simply be started again.

## Reading an arm

```
node <exp>\sent.mjs <record.json>                 what that run really sent (do this once per arm, first)
node <exp>\outcomes.mjs <arm dir> [<arm dir>...]  each run: calls in order, intent recorded, how it ended, totals
node <exp>\refused.mjs <arm dir> [...]            every refused call with the arguments the model sent
node <exp>\refused.mjs --responses <arm dir>      what each model response held, in order (SEARCH = tool search)
node <exp>\show.mjs <record.json>                 one whole conversation, replies and calls
```

## The method

1. **Predict before you run.** Write, in your report file, which outcomes your change should move, in which
   scenario, in which direction, and which must not move. Do this before the first run and do not edit it after.
2. **One mechanism per arm.** If an arm changes two things you cannot say which one worked.
3. **Compare against the same hours.** Your arms against `shared-control\control`. Earlier records are a guide.
4. **Three runs, large effects only.** 0 or 1 of 3 against 3 of 3, or a count that changes several-fold, is an
   effect. Anything smaller is "no visible effect", and say so. Do not buy more runs to rescue an unclear result.
5. **Outcomes, not paths.** An outcome is what the project ended as, what was recorded, and what the last reply
   claims. Which tool came first and how many calls it took is the path. Report both, labelled, and judge on
   outcomes.
6. **Both directions.** Each change is read on the scenario it targets and on its partner that should not
   change. A fix that helps one and breaks the other is not a fix.
7. **Attribute by mechanism.** For each thing that moved, name the sentence you changed that plausibly caused
   it and quote the evidence from a record: the call's arguments, the reply's words, the response items. Then
   say plainly what helped, what did not matter, and what hurt. A change that helps and hurts is two findings.
8. **Read the traces.** Read every failed turn and every refused call in your arms. Counts hide the reason.
9. **A failed run is a result.** Never rerun a run because it went badly, and never delete a record.
10. **No tuning loop.** Run the arms in your brief. You may add one more arm if a result directly suggests it
    and the budget allows; say why. Do not iterate wording until something passes.

## Limits

- **Spend:** one US dollar for your whole experiment. `run.ps1` counts what your folder has spent at list
  price and refuses to start a run past $0.90. If a provider error mentions a key or a quota, stop.
- **Touch nothing else.** Write only inside `exp\<your experiment>\`. Do not edit, build, commit or stage
  anything under `C:\src\JusPrin`. Do not read or print the keys file. Do not stop any process you did not
  start: other experiments' apps are running. Do not start other agents.
- **If the app will not start** (a run ends in seconds with no `LIVE USAGE` line in its log), read the end of
  that log, try the arm once more, and if it fails again stop and report what the log says.

## Your report

Write `exp\<your experiment>\REPORT.md` and return the same text as your final message:

1. The hypothesis, in one or two sentences.
2. Each arm: the exact text changed (before and after).
3. Your predictions, as written before running.
4. A table: each outcome you track, control against each arm, as counts out of 3.
5. What helped, what did not matter, what hurt, each tied to a sentence and to quoted evidence.
6. Your verdict on the hypothesis, and the wording you would keep.
7. Tokens and dollars spent, and anything that makes the result less trustworthy.

Keep it under 700 words plus the table. Say what you saw; do not round a weak result up.

Root cause (diagnosed 2026-09-25, Entire CLI 0.11.0): when the committing session has file changes to link,

`</dev/null` does not help. Commits with nothing to link skip the prompt, which is why it looked intermittent.
The log is buffered, so `.entire/logs/entire.log` shows nothing until the process exits.
Evidence: handle dump of the hung process showed a `\Device\ConDrv` handle with a blocked synchronous read.
Entire's own Pi integration prefixes agent bash commands with `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` for this exact reason.
With `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` the same hook finished in ~0.3s and added the trailer, 3 of 3 runs; without it, 3 of 3 hung.

**Why:** It looks like a slow checkpoint condense, so it is easy to wait a long time for nothing.
A separate, real slowdown also exists: an `msbuild -m` build pins all 16 cores (processor queue ~64) and every
`entire` launch then takes 5-20s. That is slow, not hung; don't confuse the two.

result.output:
**1. `defer_loading` and what the model sees**

- The guide says that for namespaces, "`defer_loading` applies to the functions inside the namespace, not to the namespace object itself."
- For a namespace or MCP server, the model initially sees only the container's name and description, not the functions inside it.
- For an individual deferred function, the model still sees its name and description. Tool search mainly defers the parameter schema.
- Tools without `defer_loading: true` are callable right away.

**2. Calling a deferred tool that hasn't been loaded**

The guide doesn't explicitly say whether such a call is refused or auto-loaded. It implies the tool is unavailable: "Tools that were not listed as part of this array will not be available to the model." Loading happens through tool search, not automatically on call.

**3. Persistence across turns and stateless use**

- For client-executed search, the guide says loaded tools persist: "The model will be able to call any of these tools in future turns," so you don't need to reload them.
- Changing the loaded set has a cost: "changing the loaded tool set will break the model's cache from that point forward."
- The guide doesn't address `store=false` or stateless operation. Its examples show two ways to continue a conversation. The JavaScript and Python examples resend the first response's output items followed by the `tool_search_output`. The Go, Java, and Ruby examples use `previous_response_id`.
- For client mode, the `tool_search_output` must echo the same `call_id` from the `tool_search_call`.
- For `additional_tools` items, the guide says to "preserve the item's position" when round-tripping conversation items manually, so the model sees the same tools at the same point.
- Hosted search output has `call_id: null`, so the `call_id` echo rule applies only to client mode.

**4. Recommendations on how many tools to keep loaded**

- The only explicit number is for namespace size: "aim to keep each namespace to fewer than 10 functions for better token efficiency and model performance."
- The guide doesn't give a recommended number of loaded tools at any one time.
- It recommends deferred loading for "a large catalog where each task needs only a few functions," and eager loading for "a small set of functions, or functions needed for most tasks."
- Mixing eager and deferred functions in Agents API sessions is "generally not recommended."
- It suggests comparing task completion, input-token usage, and latency on representative requests before choosing a default.

**5. Request format**

- **tool_search:** Add `{"type": "tool_search"}` to the `tools` array. For client-executed search, set `"execution": "client"` and provide a `description` and `parameters` schema for the search arguments.
- **Namespaces:** Use `{"type": "namespace", "name": ..., "description": ..., "tools": [...]}`. The guide says "CRM tools for customer lookup and order management" is an example of a clear namespace description.
- **defer_loading:** Set `"defer_loading": true` on each function inside the namespace. For MCP servers, set it on the MCP server tool definition.
- **Model support:** "In the Responses API, only `gpt-5.4` and later models support `tool_search`."
- The examples also set `parallel_tool_calls: false`.
- In the Agents API, add `{"type": "tool_search"}` to `agent.tools` and set `defer_loading: true` on each function to defer. MCP tools in the Agents API are discovered automatically and don't need this setup.

input.new_string:
With the `namespaces` capability, JusPrin advertises six namespaces, and each has fewer than ten deferred functions. A deferred namespace shows its name and description at the start. On OpenAI a function that is deferred individually still shows its own name and description; only its parameters arrive with the search. On OpenRouter a deferred function is hidden entirely: its documentation says "the model cannot see or call one until a search returns it", and the first journey requests (about 2,650 input tokens with 26 functions deferred) agree.

**What deferral did to the journeys (2026-10-13).** The first version of deferral kept only three reads loaded and deferred the rest, including the `core` toolset that the catalog below calls "every turn". The instructions name `intent_update`, `object_analyze`, `presets_list`, `plan_set`, `slice_report`, `slice_inspect` and `export_file`. On OpenRouter, where a deferred function is invisible, DeepSeek V4 Flash called those tools by the name it had read, without searching for them, so without their parameters: `intent_update` with `requirements`, `presets_list` with `category`, `object_analyze` with no `include`. The adapter refuses a call whose arguments miss the schema, and the third refusal in a turn ends the turn. In twelve runs of the four scenarios, 20 of 25 refused calls were such guesses, three runs ended that way, and the preparation scenario never reached a slice. Sending the six named tools loaded took refusals of those tools from 19 of 59 calls to 0 of 61 and all refusals from 25 to 5; a paragraph telling the model to search first did not stop the guesses; and removing the names from the instructions removed the behaviours with them (the model did not go looking for tools it was not told about). Loading the named tools is therefore the fix, not rewording. The records and method are in `tests/project_journey/README.md`. The built-in OpenAI route hides the function inside a namespace just as completely, and it has not yet been run on these journeys.

Short answer: no. Nothing I can find says deferral by itself makes tools less likely to be found or called correctly. The evidence points the other way for big catalogs, with three conditions attached, and our setup broke two of them.

## What the providers and the research actually say

**Deferring can improve tool choice when there are many tools.** Anthropic's engineering post reports that on its internal evaluations with large tool libraries, turning on tool search raised Opus 4's selection accuracy from 49% to 74% and Opus 4.5's from 79.5% to 88.1% ([Anthropic, advanced tool use](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/advanced-tool-use)). Its documentation says plainly that "Claude's ability to pick the right tool degrades once you exceed 30–50 available tools" ([Anthropic docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool)). An independent paper, RAG-MCP, measured the same thing the other way round: with every tool in the prompt, selection accuracy fell from 85% with five tools to 45% with twenty, and showing the model only a few retrieved tools kept it above 80% up to fifty ([RAG-MCP](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2505.03275)). The honest caveats: Anthropic's numbers are a vendor's own evaluation that nobody outside can rerun, and the paper's benchmark is small.

**But a hidden tool is only called if the model thinks to look for it.** This is the part that bit us, and it is well documented. Both Anthropic and OpenRouter tell you to keep your three to five most used tools loaded; OpenRouter's reason is that a tool needed on almost every request "costs more in search round-trips than it saves in tokens" ([OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/tool-search)). Two field reports from Claude Code describe exactly our failure. In one, the model "sometimes skips the ToolSearch step (because it 'knows' the tool name from context)", calls the deferred tool blind, and fails on the first try ([claude-code issue 60052](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/60052)). In the other, a deferred tool was used in 2 of 6 sessions, and in 6 of 6 once it was loaded from the start; naming it in the instructions made the model search for it, and the author's fix was simply to mark that tool always-loaded ([codegraph issue 1696](https://github.com/colbymchenry/codegraph/issues/1696)).

**The search step itself can miss.** Arcade tested Anthropic's search with 4,000 tools and found the right tool in the results only 56% to 64% of the time, mostly because request wording and tool names didn't match ([Arcade](https://www.arcade.dev/blog/anthropic-tool-search-4000-tools-test/)). That is a far larger catalog than ours, but it shows search is a lossy step, and our own records agree in a small way: finding slice_start took three searches in a row in several runs.

**Whether the model was trained to search matters, and nobody measures that for us.** Anthropic and OpenAI only offer tool search on specific models, which they trained for it. OpenRouter says its version "works on any model and any provider", and injects no guidance about hidden tools. DeepSeek V4 Flash, our judging model, is in that second category, and in our runs a paragraph telling it to search first barely helped. OpenAI gives no accuracy numbers at all and says to compare task completion, tokens and latency on your own requests before picking a default ([OpenAI guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-tool-search)).

## What this means for us, in plain terms

Two separate things are true at once. Stuffing many tools into the context makes the model choose worse, and deferral is the standard cure. Hiding a tool the model needs every turn, or one the instructions tell it to call by name, makes it guess, and the cure is to not hide that tool. Our first deferral did the second thing: it hid the "every turn" set and seven named tools, on a route whose model was never taught to search. The failure we saw is the predicted failure, not evidence against deferral.

Our catalog has 29 tools, right at the edge where Anthropic says choice starts to degrade and well above the "fewer than ten, don't bother" line, so some deferral is plausibly worth having. Of those 29, the records from runs where everything was visible show about 13 doing nearly all the work and the other 16 rarely or never called. Keeping those 13 loaded and deferring the rest is what both vendors' guidance describes. That is what the change in the worktree does, and I'd leave it there, unmeasured, rather than tune it further.

What is still not known, and only live runs can tell: whether the remaining 16 deferred tools are found reliably when they are needed (printer setup is the one that matters most in the preparation scenario), and whether gpt-5.4-mini on the app's own route behaves differently, since it was trained to search and DeepSeek was not. If you'd rather settle it by evidence than by the vendors' word, the two batches I proposed earlier are the way to do that, and I won't touch the code again until you say which, if either, to run.

**Bottom line:** The paper proposes Tool Attention, a middleware layer that shows each turn only a small set of relevant tool schemas. Its token reductions are measured, but its task-success, latency, cost, and quality gains are projections. The paper states that the downstream figures "are not measured on live LLM agents."

**Proposed mechanism**

- **Initial view:** The model sees a compact summary pool covering all tools, with each summary at most about 60 tokens. The paper estimates roughly 40 tokens per summary.
- **Gating:** Each user query is embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and compared to tool summaries by cosine similarity (the ISO score). Tools must clear a threshold (θ = 0.28 in the main setup) and satisfy state preconditions such as authentication.
- **Full schemas:** Full JSON schemas are loaded only for the top-k gated tools (k = 10 by default), on demand from a registry.
- **Hallucination gate:** If the model calls a tool that wasn't promoted that turn, the middleware rejects the call and returns a structured error.

**Measured results (token counts only, simulated 120-tool, six-server benchmark)**

| Method | Tokens/turn | ρ at turn 30 |
|---|---|---|
| Full-schema (naive MCP) | 47,312 | 0.24 |
| Static pruning | 11,865 | 0.56 |
| Simple retrieval | 4,082 | 0.78 |
| CLI lazy | 480 | 0.94 |
| Tool Attention | 2,368 | 0.91 |

The paper states that Tool Attention "directly reduces measured per-turn tool tokens by 95.0%" (47.3k → 2.4k). Measured token counts come from tiktoken on the constructed prompts.

**Projected results (not measured)**

- Task success: about 94% for Tool Attention vs. about 72% for full-schema (marked †).
- P50 latency: about 2.0 s vs. 4.2 s.
- Cost per task: about $0.03 vs. $0.21.
- Reasoning quality (LLM-judge, 1–5): 4.43 vs. 3.21.
- Adversarial: the gate excluded 46 of 50 poisoned descriptions. Projected poisoning success falls from 38% to 6%. The paper calls this "a defensive by-product of gating, not a targeted defense."

**Gaps relative to your question**

- **Models tested:** None. No live LLM was run.
- **Tool selection and argument accuracy:** Not reported. The paper says retrieval F1 was measured, but no F1 values appear in the text. Argument correctness is not measured; the paper only argues that full schemas help parameter population.
- **Latency:** Projected from published TTFT figures, not measured.

**Ablation (projected success):** Removing lazy loading costs about 10.3 points, the largest drop. The paper says "the model needs the full schema—not just the summary—to correctly populate parameters." Removing preconditions costs about 3.6 points.

**Limitations and failure modes the paper names**

- It is an application-layer mitigation and cannot fix protocol-level deficiencies.
- Results depend on summary quality. Cryptic tool names hurt retrieval precision.
- The evaluation uses synthetic (calibrated) workloads.
- Adversarial paraphrase: a poisoned description written to resemble benign queries could be gated in. The authors suggest pairing it with a runtime monitor.
- Ambiguous queries matched multiple similar tools, causing 14 of 29 failures (48%) on Tool Attention.
- Multi-hop tasks where the right tool becomes relevant only after an intermediate result (5 failures).
- Cross-turn state is not modeled in the main method. Re-embedding the query after each observation gave a preliminary +1.7 points on multi-hop tasks.

Yes, that is how skills work, and your version of it has already been built by others. Short answer: there is no fundamental flaw. There is one real difference between a skill and a tool that decides how to build it, and one known weakness that it shares with every kind of deferral.

**It is the same idea as skills, and people have shipped it.** Anthropic calls the skills mechanism "progressive disclosure": a name and one line in the prompt, the full text loaded when needed. Its own engineering post applies the identical idea to tools, presenting them as files the model lists and reads on demand ([Anthropic, code execution with MCP](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/code-execution-with-mcp)). Claude Code does it for me right now: deferred tools are listed by name, and I fetch a schema with a `select:` query before calling ([Claude Code docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp)). The closest match to your proposal is the Hermes agent. Someone proposed exactly your design, names and one-line descriptions up front and a `request_tool` call for the full schema, and the maintainers shipped it: the tool list stays byte-stable for the whole conversation, and deferred tools are reached through three small tools, search, describe and call. They report schema tokens per request down 49% and accuracy "flat across a 288-run three-tier A/B" ([hermes-agent issue 6839](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/6839)). A 2026 paper, Tool Attention, proposes the same shape, with short summaries always visible and full schemas loaded for a few tools, though its accuracy numbers are projected rather than measured ([arXiv 2604.21816](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.21816v1)).

**The one real difference from skills.** A skill is text: once the model has read it, it just follows it. A tool is something the model has to emit a structured call against, and most APIs only let it call tools that are in the request's tool list. So "fetch the usage, then call" needs a way for that call to get back to us. There are three ways, and this is the actual design decision:

- **Let the provider splice it in.** OpenAI and Anthropic both support "client-executed" tool search: the model calls our search tool, we answer with which tools to load, and the API inserts the full definition after the cached prefix, so caching survives ([OpenAI guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-tool-search), [Anthropic docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool)). This is your design with the provider doing the plumbing, but it only exists on those providers.
- **Change the tool list on the next request.** Works on any provider. The cost is that the tool list sits at the very front of the cached prefix, so each change throws away the cache for that conversation ([Anthropic, mid-conversation changes](https://platform.claude.com/docs/build-with-claude/mid-conversation-system-messages)). For our conversations, which are short, that is a few thousand tokens per newly loaded tool, not a disaster.
- **One generic call tool** that takes a tool name and its arguments, which is what Hermes did. Works everywhere and keeps the list stable. We lose the provider's schema enforcement on those calls, but our adapter already validates every call against the registry, so nothing reaches the app unchecked.

**The weakness it shares with all deferral.** The model still has to decide to fetch the usage before calling. With a name and a one-line description visible, that is exactly what OpenAI's per-function deferral and Claude Code already give the model, and Claude Code users still report the model calling by name without fetching the schema because it "knows" the name ([claude-code issue 60052](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/60052)). Our own runs showed the same: telling DeepSeek to search first cut blind calls from 20 to 15, not to zero. The difference with a home-made version is that we can answer a blind call with the usage itself instead of a refusal, so the model loses one round trip rather than a turn. That is the "auto-hydrate" fix the Claude Code reporter asked for and never got.

**So why would anyone not do this?** Only for ordinary reasons, none fundamental:

- It is our code to keep working across providers, where the hosted version is theirs. The guide's rule against writing our own loading mechanism was a choice made when the hosted one was picked, not a law.
- The index itself costs tokens on every request. Twenty-nine lines at forty-odd tokens each is about 1,200 tokens, always present, against roughly 8,000 for the full schemas. That is about the same saving as hosted deferral gives us.
- Every first use of a tool costs a round trip, one to two seconds.
- Loaded tools have to be remembered across turns by us. Hermes keeps a growing per-conversation set and never unloads, which is the simple answer.

**My view.** The approach is sound and well-precedented, and it has one advantage the hosted version cannot offer on OpenRouter: nothing is ever invisible, because the index names every capability in our own words, and we can tune those words the way we tune the prompt. The decision is whether to build it on the providers' client-side search, which is less code and cache-safe but provider-specific, or provider-independently with a generic call tool, which fits a product that will support several providers. Either way it needs the same live measurement as the current fix, because the "fetch before calling" step is where every version is weakest, and three runs per scenario is what tells us whether that step holds on the models we care about. I have not written any code for this and won't until you choose a direction.
